viscounty-of-limoges.t: A viscounty in the Limousin that outlasted most feudal lordships and passed by inheritance to Brittany, Albret and finally the future Henry IV.
viscounty-of-limoges.o: Viscounts appear at Limoges in the late 9th century as deputies of the counts of Poitou, who as dukes of Aquitaine claimed overlordship of the Limousin. The office became hereditary in a local family, which governed the city's castle quarter while the bishop and the abbey of Saint-Martial dominated the rest of the town.
viscounty-of-limoges.r: The viscounts were middling lords caught between Aquitaine, the Plantagenet kings and the French crown, often clashing with their own townsmen and with English overlords; Richard the Lionheart died in 1199 besieging Châlus, a castle in the viscounty. Limoges itself was known for its enamel work and as a pilgrimage centre on the road to Compostela.
viscounty-of-limoges.e: Through marriage the viscounty passed to the dukes of Brittany in 1275, then to the Blois-Penthièvre line and the house of Albret. It reached the Bourbons through Jeanne d'Albret, and when her son Henry IV became king in 1589 it was merged with the crown.

vulci.t: Wealthy Etruscan city near the Fiora river whose tombs held thousands of Greek vases and whose François Tomb preserves an Etruscan version of early Roman history.
vulci.o: Vulci, Etruscan Velch, grew from Villanovan villages on a plateau above the Fiora river, some 10 km from the coast. By the 7th and 6th centuries BCE it had become one of the richest cities of Etruria, importing luxury goods and controlling a large territory reaching towards Lake Bolsena.
vulci.r: Vulci was a major centre of bronze-working, exporting tripods, vessels and candelabra across Italy and beyond the Alps. Its tombs yielded an extraordinary number of Athenian painted vases, many excavated by Lucien Bonaparte in the 19th century. The François Tomb's paintings show the Vulcian heroes Caile and Avle Vipinas and Macstrna, whom the emperor Claudius identified with Rome's king Servius Tullius.
vulci.e: Rome defeated Vulci together with Volsinii in 280 BCE, when Tiberius Coruncanius celebrated a triumph over both. Much of its coastal land was confiscated and the Latin colony of Cosa founded there in 273 BCE. The city declined into a minor Roman town and was abandoned in the early Middle Ages.

veii.t: The richest Etruscan city near Rome, its great rival for three centuries until Marcus Furius Camillus captured it in 396 BCE after a ten-year siege.
veii.o: Veii stood on a defended tufa plateau about 16 km north of Rome, and grew from several Villanovan villages that merged into one large settlement by the 8th century BCE. It controlled the right bank of the Tiber and the salt and trade routes that Rome also wanted, making conflict between the two almost inevitable.
veii.r: Veii was famed for its craftsmen: the terracotta statues of the Portonaccio temple, including the Apollo of Veii, are among the finest Etruscan works, and Roman tradition credited a Veientine sculptor, Vulca, with the cult statue of Jupiter on the Capitol. Its territory had dense rural settlement and a sophisticated system of drainage tunnels. It was ruled by kings, notably Lars Tolumnius in the late 5th century.
veii.e: Rome and Veii fought repeatedly over Fidenae and the Tiber crossing. In 396 BCE, after a siege said to have lasted ten years, Camillus took the city, reportedly by tunnelling under its walls. Its land was divided among Roman citizens, doubling Rome's territory, and the city never recovered as an independent power.

vennicnii.t: People of north-west Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, near a headland he called Vennicnium in modern Donegal.
vennicnii.o: The Vennicnii are known only from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them on the north-western coast of Ireland, with a headland named Vennicnium Promontorium, usually identified with Bloody Foreland or another point on the Donegal coast. His Irish information came from earlier sailors' reports.
vennicnii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. The rugged coastline and uplands of Donegal supported small farming and fishing communities, and later stone forts such as the Grianan of Aileach show the importance of hilltop centres in the region.
vennicnii.e: No later source mentions the Vennicnii. Donegal later became the territory of the northern Uí Néill dynasties, including the Cenél Conaill and the rulers of the Kingdom of Ailech.

volcae-arecomici.t: Celtic people of eastern Languedoc whose sacred spring at Nemausus became the Roman city of Nîmes.
volcae-arecomici.o: The Arecomici were the eastern branch of the Volcae, a Celtic people who settled between the Rhône and the Hérault in the 3rd century BCE. Strabo records that twenty-four villages were subject to their chief town Nemausus, which grew up around a sacred spring.
volcae-arecomici.r: They lived in hilltop oppida such as Nages and Mont Vaucluse, and Nemausus had a stone tower, the Tour Magne, before the Romans arrived. They traded closely with Massalia and struck coins with Greek and Latin letters.
volcae-arecomici.e: Their land came under Rome in 121 BCE and part of it was given to Massalia by Pompey. Nemausus became a Latin colony with rich monuments, including the Maison Carrée and the aqueduct carried by the Pont du Gard.

volsinii.t: Leading Etruscan city whose shrine of Voltumna was the religious heart of the Etruscan League, crushed by Rome in 264 BCE after a slave uprising.
volsinii.o: Volsinii, Etruscan Velzna, grew on the volcanic plateau of modern Orvieto from Villanovan settlements of the early 1st millennium BCE. By the 6th century BCE it was a wealthy city with orderly necropolises such as Crocifisso del Tufo, where tombs were laid out in streets and inscribed with owners' names.
volsinii.r: Volsinii controlled a rich territory around Lake Bolsena and traded widely, as imported Greek pottery shows. Nearby lay the Fanum Voltumnae, the federal sanctuary where the twelve Etruscan peoples met each year for games, cult and council. The city was governed by an aristocracy; ancient sources say it was so rich that Rome took some 2,000 statues as booty from it.
volsinii.e: After wars with Rome in the 4th and early 3rd centuries, Volsinii's aristocrats asked Rome for help when freedmen and former slaves seized power. Rome besieged and destroyed the city in 264 BCE and moved survivors to Volsinii Novi, modern Bolsena. Rome also transferred the cult of Vertumnus to the Aventine.

vaccaei.t: A Celtic people of the Douro plains famed for sharing out land and harvests collectively, who resisted Rome until the 1st century BCE.
vaccaei.o: The Vaccaei occupied the middle Douro valley, in modern Valladolid, Palencia, Zamora and Burgos, from about the 4th century BCE. Their towns included Intercatia, Pallantia, Cauca and Pintia.
vaccaei.r: Diodorus records that they divided their land each year by lot, pooled the harvest and gave each family its share, punishing hoarding with death. They lived in large towns on the open cereal plains, and the cemetery of Las Ruedas at Pintia shows a warrior elite. They spoke a Celtic language.
vaccaei.e: Hannibal raided them in 220 BCE. In 151 BCE Lucullus massacred the people of Cauca, and later Pallantia withstood several Roman sieges. The Vaccaei fought on into the 1st century BCE, last rising in 56 BCE, before being absorbed into Hispania Citerior.

voluntii.t: People of north-east Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, often identified with the Ulaid who gave their name to Ulster.
voluntii.o: The Voluntii, or Uoluntii, appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 on the east coast of Ireland north of the Eblani, in the region of modern Counties Louth and Down. Their name is widely thought to be an early form of Ulaid, the people whose name survives in Ulster.
voluntii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions in classical sources. If the identification with the Ulaid is correct, they were the forerunners of the people whose heroic traditions, centred on Emain Macha, are preserved in the Ulster Cycle of Irish literature, though these tales were written down many centuries later.
voluntii.e: The Voluntii vanish from classical sources after Ptolemy. In early medieval Ireland the Ulaid formed the Kingdom of Ulaid, gradually pushed east of the River Bann by the Uí Néill.

viscounty-of-carcassonne.t: The Trencavel viscounties of Carcassonne, Béziers and Albi, the heart of Cathar country, destroyed by the Albigensian Crusade in 1209.
viscounty-of-carcassonne.o: In 1067 Raymond Bernard Trencavel, viscount of Albi and Nîmes, gained Carcassonne through his wife Ermengard, heiress of the counts of Carcassonne. Their son Bernard Ato IV built a principality across Carcassonne, Béziers, Albi and Razès, balancing between the counts of Toulouse and Barcelona.
viscounty-of-carcassonne.r: The Trencavels ruled from the walled city of Carcassonne, a centre of Occitan courtly culture. Their lands were the heartland of Catharism, and the viscounts tolerated the dissident church and its followers among the nobility. The Romanesque castle within Carcassonne's walls was their seat.
viscounty-of-carcassonne.e: In 1209 the Albigensian Crusade sacked Béziers and besieged Carcassonne. Raymond-Roger Trencavel surrendered and died in prison, and his lands went to Simon de Montfort. After a failed revolt in 1240 they were absorbed by the Kingdom of France.

venicones.t: People of Fife and the Tay region recorded by Ptolemy, whose lands later formed a core region of the Picts.
venicones.o: The Venicones appear in Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, generally placed in Fife and perhaps Kinross and southern Angus, between the Forth and the Tay, with a settlement called Orrea. They descended from local Iron Age communities living in hillforts, crannogs and open farmsteads on fertile lowland soils.
venicones.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or institutions. Their territory lay close to the Roman frontier: forts along the Gask Ridge and the legionary base at Carpow on the Tay, built under Severus around 208, show heavy Roman activity. Some historians think they are the people later called Maeatae, or part of them.
venicones.e: The Venicones disappear from the written record after Ptolemy. Their lands later formed the Pictish province of Fib, which gave its name to Fife, within the Kingdom of the Picts.

vascones.t: The people of Navarre and ancestors of the Basques, whose lands held Pompey's foundation of Pompaelo, modern Pamplona.
vascones.o: The Vascones lived in the upper Ebro valley and western Pyrenees, roughly modern Navarre and parts of Aragon and La Rioja, by the 3rd century BCE. They probably spoke an early form of Basque, related to Aquitanian across the mountains.
vascones.r: They lived in hill towns and villages, farming the Ebro plain and herding in the mountains. Their towns included Calagurris and later Pompaelo, and they minted coins with Iberian-script legends. They had no single ruler and were organised in local communities.
vascones.e: In the winter of 75 to 74 BCE Pompey camped in their territory, giving his name to Pompaelo. Calagurris backed Sertorius and fell in 72 BCE after a famous siege. The Vascones were absorbed into Hispania Citerior, but their language survived and later the Kingdom of Navarre arose in their land.

varduli.t: A people of the western Pyrenean coast in Gipuzkoa and Álava, among the ancestors of the Basques.
varduli.o: The Varduli lived in the area of modern Gipuzkoa and parts of Álava and Navarre in the later Iron Age, between the Caristii and the Vascones. Whether they spoke an early form of Basque or a Celtic language is debated.
varduli.r: Little is known of their society. They lived from herding, farming, fishing and the iron of their hills, and Ptolemy names towns such as Gebala and Menosca. Strabo includes them among the rough mountain peoples of the north.
varduli.e: They came under Roman rule as part of the conquest of the north completed in the Cantabrian Wars of 19 BCE, and later supplied auxiliary troops, including a cohort of Varduli that served in Britain. Their land became part of Hispania Tarraconensis.

vediantii.t: Ligurian people of the hills behind Nice whose town Cemenelum became the capital of the Roman Maritime Alps.
vediantii.o: Known from Pliny and Ptolemy, the Vediantii lived in the hills of the lower Var and Paillon valleys, behind the Greek port of Nikaia (Nice), a colony of Massalia.
vediantii.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Like other Alpine Ligurians they lived in hill forts and practised herding and farming.
vediantii.e: They were brought under Roman control in the Alpine campaigns of Augustus, and in 14 BCE their land became part of the province of Alpes Maritimae. Their settlement of Cemenelum (Cimiez, now part of Nice) became its capital, with an amphitheatre and baths that still survive.

viscounty-of-turenne.t: A self-governing viscounty in the Limousin and Quercy that kept its own estates and tax privileges until it was sold to the French crown in 1738.
viscounty-of-turenne.o: Viscounts of Turenne appear in the late 10th century, based at a castle on a hill near Brive in the Limousin. Their lands stretched into Quercy, and the family survived among the competing lords of Aquitaine by playing English and French kings against each other.
viscounty-of-turenne.r: The viscounts enjoyed unusual privileges: the right to summon their own estates, to raise taxes and, by tradition, to mint coin, with near exemption from royal taxation. In 1444 the viscounty passed to the La Tour d'Auvergne family. Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, a Huguenot leader, married into the house of La Marck and became prince of Sedan.
viscounty-of-turenne.e: In 1738, burdened by debts, Charles-Godefroy de La Tour d'Auvergne sold the viscounty to Louis XV, and it was absorbed into the Kingdom of France. Its privileges ended, and the region lost its tax exemptions.
ru: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon

vacomagi.t: People of north-east Scotland around Moray and Strathspey, to whom Ptolemy assigned four towns, among them Pinnata Castra and Tuesis.
vacomagi.o: Ptolemy's Geography of about 150 places the Vacomagi in the northern Highlands and lowlands, usually located in Moray, Strathspey and parts of Banffshire. He lists four settlements in their land, Bannatia, Tamia, Pinnata Castra and Tuesis, more than for most northern peoples, suggesting a well-populated territory.
vacomagi.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. The fertile Laich of Moray supported farming communities, and the great promontory fort at Burghead, later a major Pictish centre, has sometimes been identified with Pinnata Castra, though this is uncertain. Roman marching camps reach into the region, showing the passage of Roman armies in the late 1st and early 3rd centuries.
vacomagi.e: The Vacomagi do not appear after Ptolemy. Their lands later formed a heartland of the northern Picts, part of the Kingdom of Fortriu and the wider Kingdom of the Picts.

veliocasses.t: Belgic people of the lower Seine whose town Rotomagus became Rouen.
veliocasses.o: The Veliocasses held the Vexin and the lower Seine valley. Caesar reports that they promised warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE together with the Viromandui.
veliocasses.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their position on the Seine gave them a share of river trade to the Channel.
veliocasses.e: They submitted in 57 BCE and later sent men to relieve Alesia. Under Rome their chief town Rotomagus grew into an important river port, the origin of Rouen, later capital of the Duchy of Normandy. Their name survives in the Vexin.

volaterrae.t: Northern Etruscan city on a lofty hill, master of a large territory and famous for its alabaster urns, which later withstood Sulla for two years.
volaterrae.o: Volaterrae, Etruscan Velathri, modern Volterra, occupies a high ridge between the Cecina and Era valleys. Settled from the Villanovan period, it became one of the largest Etruscan cities by the 4th century BCE, when walls more than 7 km long enclosed the town and its fields. Its territory reached the sea and included mines and salt springs.
volaterrae.r: Volaterrae prospered from farming, salt, copper and timber. In the Hellenistic period its workshops produced hundreds of carved alabaster and tufa cinerary urns showing mythological scenes and portraits of the dead, now in the Guarnacci Museum. The Porta all'Arco, an arched city gate with sculpted heads, survives. Local families such as the Caecinae remained prominent well into Roman times.
volaterrae.e: Volaterrae became a Roman ally in the 3rd century BCE and supplied grain and timber for Scipio's fleet in 205 BCE. Having backed Marius, it held out against Sulla's siege from 82 to 79 BCE, and later became a municipium. The satirist Persius was born there, and Volterra keeps its alabaster craft.

viducasses.t: Small Gallic people of the Caen plain whose Roman town at Vieux has yielded the famous Thorigny marble.
viducasses.o: Known from Pliny and Ptolemy, the Viducasses lived south of modern Caen in lower Normandy. They were probably included among the Armorican peoples in Caesar's time.
viducasses.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers. Their chief town, Aregenua, lay at Vieux.
viducasses.e: Under Rome Aregenua became a prosperous civitas capital with baths and fine houses. The Thorigny marble, an inscription of 238 CE, honours one of its citizens, Titus Sennius Sollemnis. The civitas later merged with that of the Baiocasses.

viscounty-of-narbonne.t: The viscounty of the old Roman port of Narbonne, famed under Viscountess Ermengard as a centre of troubadour culture and Mediterranean trade.
viscounty-of-narbonne.o: Viscounts appear at Narbonne around 900 as deputies of the counts of Toulouse, who had inherited authority over the former Carolingian march of Septimania. The office became hereditary, and the viscounts shared power in the city with its powerful archbishops.
viscounty-of-narbonne.r: Narbonne was a busy port and a centre of Jewish learning. Viscountess Ermengard, who ruled from 1134 to 1192, presided over a court celebrated by troubadours and steered between Toulouse and Barcelona. Later viscounts survived the Albigensian Crusade by siding with the crusaders, while the river's shift and the silting of the port slowly cut the city's trade.
viscounty-of-narbonne.e: The viscounty passed to the house of Foix in the 15th century. In 1507 Gaston de Foix exchanged it with his uncle Louis XII for the duchy of Nemours, and it was joined to the Kingdom of France.
ru: Gaston de Foix, Duke of Nemours

vettones.t: A Celtic-speaking people of the western Meseta, known for their great hillforts and the stone boars and bulls called verracos.
vettones.o: The Vettones emerged in the second half of the first millennium BCE between the Douro and Tagus rivers, in modern Ávila, Salamanca and Cáceres and parts of Portugal. They grew out of the Iron Age Cogotas culture and were related to their Lusitanian and Celtiberian neighbours.
vettones.r: They lived in large fortified hillforts such as Las Cogotas, Ulaca and El Raso, and their economy was dominated by cattle and pig herding. Hundreds of granite sculptures of boars and bulls, the verracos, mark their territory and probably protected herds or pastures. Their society had warrior elites, and they spoke a Celtic or para-Celtic language.
vettones.e: Often allied with the Lusitanians, they resisted Rome through the 2nd century BCE and were finally subdued after campaigns including Julius Caesar's of 61 BCE. Their lands became part of the province of Lusitania, with towns such as Salmantica and Augustobriga.

votadini.t: People of south-east Scotland and Northumberland centred on Traprain Law, who lived beside Roman Britain and became the post-Roman Gododdin.
votadini.o: Ptolemy places the Votadini on the east coast between the Firth of Forth and the Tyne in the 2nd century. They descended from Iron Age communities of Lothian and the Borders, and their great hillfort at Traprain Law in East Lothian was a major centre from before the Roman arrival in the 80s.
votadini.r: Unlike neighbours such as the Selgovae, the Votadini show few signs of hostility to Rome, and many historians think they were a friendly buffer people beyond Hadrian's Wall. Roman goods reached Traprain Law in quantity, culminating in the Traprain Law Treasure, a hoard of cut Roman silver buried in the early 5th century, perhaps a payment or subsidy. Their economy rested on mixed farming.
votadini.e: After Roman rule ended, the Votadini developed into the Kingdom of Gododdin, centred on Din Eidyn, Edinburgh, whose warriors are celebrated in the Welsh poem Y Gododdin. Their name in its Welsh form, Guotodin, carried the people into the early medieval period.

viromandui.t: Belgic people of the upper Somme whose name lives on in the Vermandois and the town of Vermand.
viromandui.o: The Viromandui lived in the upper valleys of the Somme and Oise, between the Nervii, Ambiani and Suessiones. Caesar records that they promised ten thousand warriors to the Belgic league of 57 BCE.
viromandui.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or institutions. Excavations at Vermand have revealed a large fortified site of the period.
viromandui.e: They fought beside the Nervii and Atrebates at the Battle of the Sabis in 57 BCE and were defeated. Under Rome their chief town became Augusta Viromanduorum (Saint-Quentin), and the medieval County of Vermandois kept their name.

velabri.t: People of south-west Ireland recorded by Ptolemy, usually placed on the Atlantic coast of Kerry beside the Iverni.
velabri.o: The Velabri are known only from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them on the south-west coast of Ireland, south of the Gangani (Ireland) and west of the Iverni, roughly in modern County Kerry. Ptolemy's information on Ireland came from earlier reports by sailors along the Atlantic coast.
velabri.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers, settlements or customs. The peninsulas of Kerry were a land of stone forts, promontory forts and pastoral farming, and the region later produced many ogham stones, showing that Irish-speaking communities with strong lineage traditions lived there by the 5th century.
velabri.e: The Velabri do not appear in any later source, and no Irish population name has been securely matched with theirs. Their region later formed part of the Kingdom of Munster and the lands of peoples such as the Corcu Duibne and the Ciarraige Luachra.

vocontii.t: Confederation of the pre-Alps of the Drôme and Vaucluse that became an allied state of Rome, with its towns at Vaison and Die.
vocontii.o: The Vocontii held the mountains and valleys between the Rhône and the Alps, from the Drôme to Mont Ventoux. They were a league of smaller communities. Rome campaigned against them under Marcus Fulvius Flaccus in 124 BCE, during the first wars in Transalpine Gaul.
vocontii.r: After submission they kept unusual autonomy as a federated people, with two capitals, Vasio (Vaison-la-Romaine) and Lucus Augusti (Luc-en-Diois), later replaced by Dea Augusta (Die). The historian Pompeius Trogus came from a Vocontian family granted Roman citizenship.
vocontii.e: Their land was incorporated into Gallia Narbonensis. Vaison-la-Romaine preserves one of the largest excavated Roman towns in France, with houses, a theatre and a bridge still in use.

veneti.t: Seafaring Gallic people of southern Brittany who controlled Atlantic trade with Britain until Caesar destroyed their fleet in 56 BCE.
veneti.o: The Veneti held the coast of the Morbihan, a landscape of tidal inlets and promontories, with Darioritum (Vannes) as their later chief town. They dominated the sea routes between Armorica and Britain and were the strongest of the Armorican peoples.
veneti.r: Caesar describes their tall oak ships with flat bottoms, iron bolts and leather sails, built to ride Atlantic storms, and their towns set on headlands cut off by the tide. They levied tolls on other seafarers and grew rich on trade in tin and goods with Britain.
veneti.e: In 56 BCE they detained Roman officers sent for grain, and Caesar built a fleet on the Loire. Decimus Brutus defeated them in a calm, probably in Quiberon Bay, by cutting their rigging with hooked poles. Caesar executed their council and sold the people into slavery; Vannes keeps their name.

vetulonia.t: Early Etruscan power in the metal-rich hills of northern Etruria, which Roman tradition credited as the source of the fasces and other symbols of office.
vetulonia.o: Vetulonia, Etruscan Vatluna, grew on a hill overlooking the former Lake Prile, then a lagoon open to the sea, in the 9th and 8th centuries BCE. Its wealth came from the copper, iron and silver of the nearby Colline Metallifere, and it was one of the leading Etruscan centres of the 8th and 7th centuries BCE.
vetulonia.r: Rich 'circle tombs' and great tumuli such as the Pietrera reveal an aristocracy enriched by metals and trade with Sardinia and the eastern Mediterranean. Its goldsmiths excelled in granulation. The 'Tomb of the Lictor' contained an iron double axe with rods, and the Roman poet Silius Italicus wrote that Rome borrowed the fasces, curule chair and purple-bordered toga from Vetulonia.
vetulonia.e: Vetulonia declined from the 6th century BCE as Populonia and Rusellae grew. It revived in the Hellenistic period, minting coins, and passed under Roman control in the early 3rd century BCE, later becoming a municipium. Its exact location was only confirmed in the 19th century; the village of Colonna di Buriano took the ancient name in 1887.

volcae-tectosages.t: Celtic people of Toulouse, kin of the Galatians of Anatolia, whose sacred gold was seized by a Roman consul in 106 BCE.
volcae-tectosages.o: The Volcae were a Celtic people who settled in Languedoc in the 3rd century BCE. The Tectosages held the western part around Tolosa (Toulouse) on the Garonne. Other bands of the same name joined the migrations into the Balkans and Anatolia, where the Galatian Tectosages settled around Ancyra.
volcae-tectosages.r: Tolosa controlled the corridor between the Mediterranean and the Atlantic. Strabo describes a rich sanctuary where gold and silver were sunk in sacred lakes. They became allies of Rome after the conquest of the Province in 121 BCE.
volcae-tectosages.e: In 107 BCE they rebelled with the help of the migrating Cimbri and Tigurini. The consul Quintus Servilius Caepio retook Tolosa in 106 BCE and seized its treasure, the gold of Tolosa, which vanished on the way to Rome. Their land became part of Gallia Narbonensis.

vellavi.t: Gallic people of the Velay highlands around Le Puy, dependents of the Arverni.
vellavi.o: The Vellavi held the volcanic uplands of the upper Loire, in the modern Haute-Loire. Caesar lists them among the peoples under the authority of the Arverni.
vellavi.r: Nothing is known of their rulers. Their territory lay on the routes from the Arverni lands south towards the Mediterranean.
vellavi.e: They followed the Arverni into the revolt of 52 BCE. Under Rome they formed a civitas with its chief town at Ruessium (Saint-Paulien), later moved to Anicium (Le Puy-en-Velay). Their name survives in the Velay.

vasates.t: Aquitanian people south of the Garonne whose town Cossium became Bazas, centre of the Bazadais.
vasates.o: The Vasates, called Vocates by Caesar, lived south of the middle Garonne in the modern Gironde. They surrendered to Publius Crassus in 56 BCE with the other Aquitanian peoples.
vasates.r: No rulers or institutions are known. Their territory lay between the Garonne valley and the Landes forest, on the route from Burdigala to the Pyrenees.
vasates.e: Under Rome their chief town Cossium was renamed Civitas Vasatica, from which comes Bazas. The poet Ausonius had family links with the town, and its district kept the name Bazadais.
